3671: Wang Dongxing said at the meeting that these two lines were Chairman Hua's idea.
3672: Coming out of the meeting, a young cadre from the ACFTU caught up with you and asked whether these two lines meant that nothing the Chairman had decided could be changed. You said, that is what they mean. He said, Comrade Xiaoping's case was also decided by the Chairman. You said, that is why hands have to go up at the July plenum.
3675: first secretary of the Municipal Party Committee
3676: former first secretary of the Municipal Party Committee
3677: deputy head of the Central Cultural Revolution Group
3678: director of the Shanghai People's Commune
3679: chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee
3681: Vice Premier of the State Council
3682: head of the Central Cultural Revolution Group
3683: secretary of the Municipal Party Secretariat
3684: vice chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee
3686: head of the Municipal Party Committee writing team
3693: chairman of the Municipal Federation of Trade Unions
3694: political commissar of the Fourth Air Army
3695: commander of the Nanjing Military Region
3699: Chairman of the CPC Central Committee
3700: head of the Municipal Party Committee writing group
3701: Party branch secretary, Peking University Philosophy Department
3702: former director of the General Logistics Department
3703: Essays written with a brush on large sheets of paper and posted on walls. Anyone could write one, to expose or criticize others. In the Cultural Revolution this was the main way ordinary people spoke in public. Whom a poster named, and whether it was signed, could shape a person's later fate.
3704: This was Mao Zedong's verdict on Nie Yuanzi's big-character poster. In June 1966 the poster was broadcast nationwide and printed in the People's Daily. From this people understood that the masses could openly criticize the Party organization of their own unit.
3705: The essay column written jointly in Beijing by Deng Tuo, Wu Han and Liao Mosha. In May 1966 the three were labeled “anti-Party and anti-socialist” and criticized across the country. Early in the movement, the posters in many units dared to attack only distant targets like this and left their own leaders alone.
3706: Teams of cadres that Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping sent in June 1966 to lead the movement in schools and factories. The work teams mostly turned on the masses who had criticized the Party committees. At the end of July Mao Zedong criticized them for suppressing the masses, and from then on those who had opposed the work teams had grounds to rebel.
3707: A catch-all term in the Cultural Revolution for all kinds of “class enemies”. Landlords, rightists and people with historical problems could all be counted, and the scope could be widened at will. Once the movement focused on this, those persecuted were mostly ordinary people, and the cadres in power came through untouched.
3708: Every urban worker had a personnel dossier, kept by the work unit and never shown to the person. Joining the Party, promotion and housing all depended on it. Early in the Cultural Revolution, things the masses had said were compiled into materials and put in dossiers, later called “black materials”. What the rebels wanted most urgently was to destroy them.
3709: The Central Committee's August 1966 decision on the Cultural Revolution, sixteen points in all. It said the targets were power holders within the Party taking the capitalist road, and that the masses must not be labeled counterrevolutionaries. Rebels often used it to protect themselves.
3710: The Central Committee's theory journal, run during the Cultural Revolution by Chen Boda and others. Together with the People's Daily and the PLA Daily it was called the “two papers and one journal”. Its editorials often carried the latest thinking at the very top.
3711: A term the Central Committee formally put forward in October 1966 for the early practice of sending work teams and persecuting the masses. Once it appeared, people persecuted earlier could demand rehabilitation, and the cadres who had persecuted them had to make self-criticisms. Because of this, many grassroots rebels went from being the persecuted to being the ones on the right side.
3712: Mass organizations made up mostly of college and middle school students, formed from 1966. From August Mao Zedong received them in Tiananmen many times, and students could ride trains free to link up across the country. Beijing students linking up in Shanghai pushed Shanghai's workers to rebel.
3713: An honorary title awarded in factories in the 1960s, requiring good political thinking, task completion, discipline, mutual help and study. Those who won it were usually activists everyone in the workshop recognized.
3714: A political charge. Once labeled, a person could not hold his head up at work, a record stayed in his dossier, and his family suffered too. Early in the Cultural Revolution, many people who had only criticized grassroots Party organizations were labeled this way.
3715: Studying the Selected Works of Mao Zedong. In the 1960s the whole country promoted studying Mao's works, and factory workshops commonly had study groups. Criticizing a Party organization for not studying Mao's works seriously was the safest criticism there was, and at the time it could still get you labeled anti-Party.
3716: Full name Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters, founded in November 1966, with Wang Hongwen as its main leader. It was the first citywide workers' rebel organization in the country to win clear support from the Central Cultural Revolution Group. Historically, over the next ten years its core members entered revolutionary committees at every level, and after 1976 its members were investigated one by one.
3717: The Shanghai Municipal Party Committee's stance on the Workers' General Headquarters. It would not take part, would not recognize it and would not support it. The committee based this on central rules of the time that workers could not link up across factories or form cross-industry organizations. To the rebels, this amounted to calling them illegal.
3718: Anting is a small station on the Shanghai-Nanjing Railway outside Shanghai. On November 10, 1966, workers of the Workers' General Headquarters took a train north to petition in Beijing, and the train was stopped here. Then some people stopped passing trains. This became known as the “Anting Incident”. Which trains were stopped, and for how long, is still disputed.
3719: The workers' organization that protected the Party committees, full name “Shanghai Headquarters of the Workers' Scarlet Guards for Defending Mao Zedong Thought”. At the end of November 1966, seeing the Workers' General Headquarters rise in rebellion, the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee backed another group of workers in organizing. The committee cleared offices for them, its leaders spoke at their founding rally, and factory Party committees helped mobilize. Most members were Party members, Youth League members, model workers and old master workers. They trusted the Party and listened to the Party committees. In their eyes the Party committee was the Party, and opposing the Party committee was opposing the Party. Before 1966 everyone accepted this, so they felt they were on the right side. They claimed 800,000 members, more than WGHQ.
3720: The body set up in May 1966 to lead the Cultural Revolution, with Chen Boda as head, Jiang Qing as first deputy head, and Zhang Chunqiao and others as deputy heads. In name it answered to the Politburo Standing Committee. In practice it directed the whole movement. Whichever mass organization it backed, that organization's fate was largely decided.
3721: The Central Committee's leading body for East China, ranked above the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. During the Anting Incident, both the East China Bureau and the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee were against recognizing the Workers' General Headquarters.
3722: The five demands the Workers' General Headquarters put forward after the Anting Incident, which Zhang Chunqiao signed on November 13, 1966. The first was recognition of WGHQ as a legal organization. The others included having the Municipal Party Committee bear responsibility for the incident and having Cao Diqiu make a public self-criticism. An hour before he signed, Zhang Chunqiao had agreed with the Central Committee's position of not recognizing WGHQ.
3723: The article of the 1954 Constitution granting citizens freedom of speech, assembly, association and so on. After the Anting Incident, Mao Zedong read this article out at a meeting, asked whether workers had freedom of association, and said Zhang Chunqiao was right on the Shanghai question. Historically, a little over a month later, the same article was not used to protect the Scarlet Guards.
3724: A signed list left when bread was delivered to the workers on the train on the day of the Anting Incident. The Municipal Party Committee and the Railway Bureau held the train while also sending food to those aboard. In the later purge, such receipts were used to determine who had been at Anting.
3725: At the end of November 1966 the student organization Red Revolutionaries demanded that its tabloid be distributed inside the Liberation Daily. The paper refused, and the Red Revolutionaries stormed the building. The Workers' General Headquarters came to support them, and the Scarlet Guards surrounded them outside. The standoff lasted eight days and nine nights, and the paper stopped publishing. This was the first time the two worker factions in Shanghai faced each other by the thousands.
3726: The Red Guard Revolutionary Committee of Shanghai's colleges and universities, mostly students from Fudan and Jiaotong University. It was the most influential student rebel organization in Shanghai in the fall and winter of 1966. During the Liberation Daily Incident it stood with the Workers' General Headquarters. Historically, in January 1967 it led the call to “Bombard Zhang Chunqiao”, was put down by WGHQ, and then broke up.
3727: The tabloid run by the Red Revolutionaries. Mass organizations put out hundreds of tabloids during the Cultural Revolution. They were people's main source of news then, and also tools the factions used to attack each other.
3728: The eight demands the Scarlet Guards put to Cao Diqiu on December 23, 1966. The first was recognition of the Scarlet Guards as a revolutionary mass organization, and Cao Diqiu signed. The next day the Municipal Party Committee decided the signature was a mistake, and on the 25th Cao Diqiu publicly declared it void. The Scarlet Guards then went to Kangping Road to demand an answer.
3729: The rebels' name for the conservatives, meaning people who protected “emperors” such as the capitalist roaders. Historically, after 1967 being called a royalist meant being seen as on the wrong side, and core members were struggled against and locked up. Most of those called this were Party members, model workers and workshop activists.
3730: Kangping Road was where the Shanghai Municipal Party Secretariat sat. On December 28, 1966, nearly 20,000 Scarlet Guards went in to petition, demanding an explanation for voiding the signature. Historically, before dawn on the 30th the Workers' General Headquarters and other organizations stormed in. More than 300 Scarlet Guards were seized and 91 were seriously injured.
3731: An order the Workers' General Headquarters issued on December 31, 1966, to seize Scarlet Guard leaders at every level and hand them to the Public Security Bureau. One mass organization issuing arrest orders against another shows that by then the public security organs had lost control.
3732: After Kangping Road, about 10,000 Scarlet Guards set out north on foot to petition in Beijing. On December 31 pursuing rebels stopped them at Kunshan in Jiangsu. Kunshan is the next stop after Anting. A month and a half earlier the rebels had been stopped. This time it was the conservatives.
3733: The process by which Shanghai's rebels seized the power of the Municipal Party Committee and city government in January 1967, officially called the “January Revolution” at the time. The rebels first took over the newspapers, then held a mass rally to overthrow the Municipal Party Committee. The Central Committee then sent a telegram of congratulations, and power seizures followed across the country. The Central Cultural Revolution Group guided this power seizure from above throughout.
3734: A notice the Workers' General Headquarters and other rebel organizations published in the papers on January 9, 1967. It cast workers' demands for back pay, for making temporary workers permanent and for sent-down people to return to the city as “economism” stirred up by capitalist roaders in the Municipal Party Committee, and it called on everyone to “grasp revolution, promote production”. The Central Committee called it entirely correct.
3735: A term used in Shanghai in January 1967 to criticize workers who demanded money, permanent status or a return to the city. Some unit leaders did hand out money recklessly to protect themselves, and banks saw runs. But many demands were real grievances piled up for years, and the term condemned both together.
3736: An employment practice in 1960s factories. Temporary and contract workers did the same work as regular workers but had no wage grade, labor insurance or dossier, and could be dismissed at any time. They were among the first to rebel early in the Cultural Revolution. In early 1967 they demanded to be made permanent, and this was labeled economism.
3737: The new government founded in Shanghai on February 5, 1967, with Zhang Chunqiao as director and Wang Hongwen and others as deputy directors. Its declaration said leaders would later be elected on Paris Commune principles. Historically, it never held an election. It lasted only 19 days before being renamed the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee.
3738: The practice of the 1871 Paris Commune. Officials were elected, could be recalled at any time, and earned no more than a skilled worker. The Sixteen Points explicitly called for such elections. In the Cultural Revolution these principles were used to mobilize the masses. Historically, when the new governments were set up, they were not carried out.
3739: The local governments set up after power seizures in the Cultural Revolution, made up of representatives of the army, cadres and mass organizations. On February 24, 1967 the Shanghai People's Commune was renamed the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee without changing a single member. Provinces across the country then set them up one after another.
3740: The way revolutionary committees were formed, with the army, cadres and mass organizations each sending representatives. It brought rebel leaders into the new government and also used the army and veteran cadres to keep them in check.
3741: The “Second Regiment of the Workers' General Headquarters” led by Geng Jinzhang. In name it belonged to WGHQ, but in fact it did not take orders from Wang Hongwen. In early 1967 it claimed 500,000 to 600,000 members. Historically, in February 1967 Wang Hongwen had Geng Jinzhang trapped and seized, and the Second Regiment soon broke up.
3742: A major Shanghai newspaper. In November 1965 it ran Yao Wenyuan's article attacking “Hai Rui Dismissed from Office”, and the Cultural Revolution started from there. On January 4, 1967 the rebels took it over. This was the first step of the January Storm.
3743: A notice the Workers' General Headquarters issued on February 11, 1967, accusing Geng Jinzhang of building his own fiefdom and splitting the organization, and ruling that WGHQ would have no regiments under it. The next day Geng Jinzhang organized more than 100 trucks to parade through the streets, shouting “Down with Wang Hongwen”. Historically, two weeks later Geng Jinzhang was seized.
3744: A rebel faction at the Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant, made up mostly of young workers and ordinary people. The plant's other faction, The East Is Red, followed the Workers' General Headquarters. On August 4, 1967 large numbers of people surrounded the plant and took the Liansi building. This became known as “smashing the Liansi”, the largest armed fighting of the Cultural Revolution in Shanghai. Both sides said they were the true rebels.
3745: The “Support-Liansi Liaison Station” founded in the spring of 1967. It brought together workers and students who opposed the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee and the Workers' General Headquarters, and it called for a “second great upheaval” in Shanghai. Among them were people who had been persecuted and former Scarlet Guards. Historically, at the end of July WGHQ seized more than 30 of its leaders, and it broke up.
3746: The central meeting held in Beijing in October 1968 that expelled Liu Shaoqi from the Party for good. Wang Hongwen attended as a Shanghai delegate without a vote, and on the closing day Mao Zedong introduced him in front of everyone. On the day a factory security officer was introduced to the meeting, the head of state was expelled from the Party.
3747: The Ninth National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in April 1969, which wrote Lin Biao into the Party Constitution as Mao Zedong's successor. At this congress Wang Hongwen, 34, was elected a Central Committee member.
3748: On September 13, 1971 Lin Biao fled by plane and crashed in Mongolia. Afterward the whole country purged Lin Biao's people, and Wang Weiguo in Shanghai was arrested. The successor's place was left empty, which mattered a great deal for Wang Hongwen.
3749: Full name Workers' Mao Zedong Thought Propaganda Team. From July 1968 these teams of workers were sent into schools, government offices and research institutes to run things. Wang Hongwen was in charge of Shanghai's Workers' Propaganda Team, which at one point numbered 100,000. In those years these were the people intellectuals dealt with most.
3750: A biography in the Book of the Later Han. Liu Penzi was a cowherd boy in a rebel army at the end of the Western Han. He was made emperor by drawing lots, served as a puppet for two years, surrendered, and died a natural death. In 1973 Mao Zedong told Wang Hongwen to read it. People differ on what he meant.
3751: The Tenth National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in August 1973. Wang Hongwen gave the report on revising the Party Constitution and was then elected Vice Chairman of the Central Committee at 38, nominally third in rank. Outsiders widely saw him as the next successor after Lin Biao.
3752: In 1974 Mao Zedong criticized Jiang Qing, Wang Hongwen, Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan for forming a little faction, and later told Wang Hongwen, “Don't form a gang of four.” Historically, after October 1976 this became the official verdict on them. Wang Hongwen was the youngest of the four and the only one of worker origin.
3753: The Fengqing was a 10,000-ton oceangoing freighter built in Shanghai. The Ministry of Transport thought its main engine was faulty, and the Shanghai side called this worshipping foreign things and fawning on foreigners. In October 1974 Jiang Qing used it at a Politburo meeting to press Deng Xiaoping to declare himself, and Deng Xiaoping walked out. The next day Wang Hongwen flew to Changsha to complain to Mao Zedong.
3754: In October 1974 Wang Hongwen flew to Changsha without telling the other Politburo members, to complain to Mao Zedong about Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping. Mao Zedong turned around and criticized him, telling him to get along with Deng Xiaoping and to stop siding with Jiang Qing. Historically, this is seen as Wang Hongwen's political turning point.
3755: A big-character poster of over 20,000 characters put up on a Guangzhou street in November 1974, signed Li Yizhe, a name made from one character of each of three people's names. It called for socialist democracy and rule of law while also praising the Cultural Revolution. Guangdong organized hundreds of criticism meetings against it. Historically, after 1976 it was ruled a counterrevolutionary case, and it was rehabilitated in 1979.
3756: Short for speaking out freely, airing views fully, holding great debates, writing big-character posters. In the Cultural Revolution they were used first of all to persecute people. In 1975 they were written into the Constitution as rights of the masses. Historically, in 1980 they were removed from the Constitution again.
3757: Shadian is a Hui village in Yunnan. During the Cultural Revolution its mosque was closed, and the Hui petitioned many times to restore their religious freedom. At the end of July 1975 troops surrounded Shadian and nearby villages, and about 1,600 civilians died. Historically, accounts differ on who gave the order. The case was rehabilitated in 1979.
3758: From 1975 Wang Hongwen worked on Shanghai's militia, and by 1976 it was said to have several divisions. Historically, after October 1976 the official account called it the Gang of Four's “second armed force” for an armed rebellion, while others say the militia was built according to central documents. Both accounts agree that Shanghai prepared to resist in October and stood down a few days later.
3759: Around Qingming in 1976, crowds in Beijing and elsewhere used mourning for Zhou Enlai to criticize Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen. On the evening of April 5 militia and police cleared the square. Many were beaten and arrested, and it was labeled a counterrevolutionary incident at the time. Historically, it was rehabilitated in 1978.
3760: A code agreed on when Shanghai sent people to Beijing for news in October 1976. If all was normal, they would say everyone was fine. If something not serious happened, they would say someone felt unwell. If the central leaders really had been arrested, they would say myocardial infarction. The word that came back over the phone was myocardial infarction.
3761: The court set up from late 1980 to early 1981 to try ten principal defendants of the Lin Biao and Jiang Qing cliques. Wang Hongwen faced five charges, including the Kangping Road Incident and the armed fighting with the Shanghai Diesel Liansi. The Anting Incident was not among them. He pleaded guilty to all of them and was sentenced to life imprisonment.
3762: Exposure materials the Central Committee issued from December 1976 for nationwide study, listing the problems of Wang Hongwen and the other three. Wang Hongwen's part said he demanded color TVs, cameras and other goods from Shanghai. These materials were prepared for criticism. They were never independently verified and were not court evidence.
3763: A slogan Jiang Qing put forward in the summer of 1967, literally meaning attack with words, defend with arms. When the Liansi was smashed in Shanghai, the attackers wore wicker helmets and carried spears and clubs. This force was later turned into the workers' militia.
3764: A document the State Planning Commission drafted in 1975. It called for overhauling leadership bodies, setting up rules and regulations, and guarding against sabotage in the name of rebellion. It was one of the documents of Deng Xiaoping's rectification. Historically, in 1976 it was denounced as a “big poisonous weed”.
3765: A national organization founded in Beijing in November 1966 by contract and temporary workers, Quanhongzong for short. In January 1967 it signed a notice with the Ministry of Labor and others forbidding arbitrary dismissal of temporary workers, and two days later the Central Cultural Revolution Group voided it. Historically, in February it was labeled a reactionary organization, and its leaders around the country were arrested.
3766: Measured by Party membership, cadre post and army service, you have the strongest claim. If you become the head, you are also the first to be held to account when things go wrong.
3767: Little Pan is young and bold, and people respect his nerve. You step back to number two. You take less of the top risk, and your words carry less weight too.
3768: With no single head, every factory has a share and no one outranks anyone. But when the Municipal Party Committee or the Central Committee wants someone to talk to, there is no one who can make the call.
3769: Taking the people from the rally to the gate of the Municipal Party Committee means confronting the committee face to face. Whoever leads them is the easiest to go after once back at the factory.
3770: Going over the Municipal Party Committee straight to the Central Committee amounts to saying the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee doesn't count. Workers leaving their factories for Beijing count as deserting their posts and will be blamed for sabotaging production.
3771: If you do not confront the Municipal Party Committee and go back to work, no one can fault you. But the organization is not yet recognized, and once it breaks up, the people at each factory will be persecuted on their own.
3772: Standing with the people on the tracks makes you part of stopping the train. You are a Party member and a security section officer, so if you go down there you will be taken for a leader.
3773: You have a part in stopping the train, but not at the front. The people on the tracks treat you as one of their own, and if it comes to blame, yours is a bit lighter than the leaders'.
3774: If you stand on the platform urging people back, those on the tracks will see you as on the Municipal Party Committee's side. When stopping the train is investigated, you will have no part in it.
3775: Saying in front of everyone that the people on the tracks are holding passengers hostage is what the Municipal Party Committee would say. Once you say it, the people on the tracks will treat you as an enemy.
3776: If you don't say it, the people on the tracks won't hate you. But if you just stand on the platform, neither those on the train nor those on the tracks can tell which side you are on.
3777: Let Little Pan stand up to the man from the Central Committee while you take no position, and you offend neither side. But you will not be among those who decide things at the negotiating table.
3778: Backing the Central Committee's view first and then raising conditions puts you on the side that can negotiate. The six people in the room who refuse to go back will say you have gone soft.
3779: Siding with the majority in the room means standing up to the man from the Central Committee face to face. The people on the train will trust you. The Central Committee will see you as the side that won't obey.
3780: With more than 100 people from the No. 17 Mill going back together, there are enough of you not to fear being surrounded at the mill. Other factories have only a few people each, and once you leave they lose their support.
